sections.overview: This poison frog is native to Colombia’s Pacific-facing Chocó forests, where it walks and hops through damp leaf litter. Its striking yellow or orange body and dark limbs warn predators of defensive skin alkaloids.
sections.identification: Reported adult lengths vary by source, around 32–43 millimetres from snout to vent; females are usually slightly larger. The back and upper limbs are golden yellow to orange, while the legs are mainly black, sometimes spotted blue or gold. Four forelimb fingers and five hind toes have adhesive tips for climbing. A reliable adult body-mass range was not found in the consulted sources; the measurements below are snout-to-vent lengths, not total length.
sections.habitat: It inhabits humid tropical forests on Colombia’s Pacific slope, from Chocó to western Andean foothills. Records span roughly 400–1,500 metres; it shelters and forages in damp leaf litter near streams.
sections.diet: Adults hunt tiny leaf-litter arthropods, including ants, termites and small beetles, snapping them up with a long, sticky tongue. Tadpoles feed on insect larvae and detritus. Defensive alkaloids in wild frogs are acquired from food rather than manufactured by the frog, although the precise dietary source of batrachotoxin remains unresolved.
sections.behavior: By day it moves in short hops, foraging on the forest floor. Males call with trills or buzzes, and rivals may wrestle over calling sites.
sections.reproduction: Breeding occurs in the rainy season. After courtship, the female lays about 4–30 eggs in a moist sheltered place; fertilization is external, and a parent guards the clutch. At hatching, a parent carries tadpoles on its back to small pools, where they feed and metamorphose before returning to land.
sections.ecology: Batrachotoxin is a steroidal alkaloid neurotoxin: it holds voltage-gated sodium channels open, disrupting electrical signals in nerves, muscles and the heart. The frog stores defensive compounds in skin glands; wild frogs carry them, whereas captive-bred frogs generally lack detectable batrachotoxins when their food lacks the relevant alkaloids.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List assessment published in 2017 classified the species as Endangered. Forest conversion and degradation, including clearing, farming, mining and pollution, threaten its restricted Colombian range.
